what_it_is.body: Polygon PoS is an EVM sidechain with its own validator consensus. Bor executes transactions and Heimdall-v2 coordinates validators and checkpoints state to Ethereum. That checkpointing does not make Polygon PoS an Ethereum rollup: Polygon validators still order and validate the chain, so its security and activity must be measured separately.

what_happened.body: Polygon has meaningful payment and trading activity, but its capital and token have not recovered their prior peaks. TVL was $800.28 million, down 91.92% from the June 2021 series peak. Dollar stablecoins were $3.08 billion and thirty-day DEX volume was $7.29 billion. POL was $0.073, about 94.34% below its recorded high.

why_this_outcome.body: Low-cost EVM compatibility, Ethereum-era distribution and broad wallet support kept Polygon useful after the 2021 cycle. Management then narrowed the story toward stablecoin payments and the Open Money Stack. That created real transaction demand, but constant repositioning, competing L2s and weak POL price performance made it harder for the market to value Polygon as the default Ethereum scaling venue.

strategic_choices.body: Polygon kept its PoS sidechain, migrated MATIC to POL and directed newer upgrades toward fast, predictable payments. Rio changed validator and finality mechanics; Lisovo added a sponsored-gas program and fee controls. POL emissions fund validators and a community treasury. These choices favor distribution and payment throughput, but they add continuing dilution and do not inherit rollup security by default.

operating_model.body: Users submit EVM transactions to Bor. A stake-weighted producer set builds blocks, while Heimdall-v2 validators run consensus and submit checkpoints to Ethereum contracts. POL pays gas and is staked by validators. Governance starts through public PIPs and off-chain discussion, but network upgrades still require software adoption by validators and node operators.

token_and_value_capture.body: POL pays transaction fees, secures Polygon PoS through staking and funds validator rewards. After June 2025 the documented effective emission rate is 2% a year: 1% for validators and 1% for the community treasury, subject to governance. Fees can burn POL, but activity must exceed issuance for supply to contract. POL market capitalization and fully diluted value were each about $779.14 million.

counterfactual.body: Polygon could have converted the PoS chain into a rollup with Ethereum-enforced proofs, trading more inherited security for different cost and operating constraints. It could also have kept a broader general-purpose positioning instead of concentrating on payments. Either path might have reduced narrative churn, but neither guarantees retained users, liquidity or token demand.

risks_and_unknowns.body: The main risks are validator concentration, bridge and checkpoint failures, recurring token dilution, competition from Ethereum L2s and dependence on payment partners. Aggregate volume does not reveal retained users or profitable demand. We also lack a current beneficial-owner map of validators and a reconciled statement showing how much payment activity produces sustainable POL burn or treasury revenue.

lifecycle.body: Polygon is mixed. It remains a large payments and trading chain with $3.08 billion of stablecoins and $7.29 billion of thirty-day DEX volume. The 91.92% TVL drawdown and 94.34% POL price drawdown show that activity has not restored prior capital or token expectations. This is an operating network with a credible niche, not a dead chain or a clean return to peak leadership.

outlook_and_watch.body: The outlook improves if payment volume produces repeat users, stablecoin balances, fee burn and partner growth without larger subsidies. It weakens if activity migrates to L2s, validator control concentrates or POL issuance consistently outruns burns. Watch payment transaction cohorts, stablecoin net flows, DEX volume, fees, POL burn versus issuance, validator ownership and shipped progress on the payments roadmap.

what_it_is.body: Robinhood Chain is an Arbitrum-based Ethereum Layer 2 built for tokenized assets, trading and consumer finance. It posts data to Ethereum and uses ETH for gas. Robinhood operates the sequencer, while a Security Council and a small permissioned validator set control important recovery and upgrade paths. Robinhood stock and stock tokens are products on the chain, not a native chain token.

what_happened.body: Public mainnet launched on July 1, 2026 and attracted rapid early liquidity. At review, TVL was $401.01 million, dollar stablecoins were $558.94 million and thirty-day DEX volume was $14.72 billion. That volume was up 2,223% from the provider comparison period, but the chain was only about one month old, so the percentage is a launch-base effect rather than evidence of durable retention.

why_this_outcome.body: Robinhood brought an existing brokerage brand, regulated-market distribution and tokenized-stock inventory to a purpose-built chain. That is a stronger acquisition channel than launching an L2 with no captive users. The same integration concentrates control and creates legal and product dependency: if Robinhood does not route users or assets on-chain, the network has little independent history to fall back on.

strategic_choices.body: Robinhood chose an Arbitrum Orbit rollup instead of building a new consensus network, ETH instead of a native gas token, a first-come-first-served sequencer and a curated launch around tokenized assets. It also kept validation permissioned and gave an eight-member Security Council upgrade and emergency powers. These choices speed launch and simplify user experience, but they leave trust and censorship exposure.

operating_model.body: Robinhood operates the sequencer that orders transactions. Arbitrum Nitro software executes the chain, transaction data is posted in Ethereum blobs and BoLD handles disputes. Only allowlisted validators can participate today; documentation names two. Routine Security Council changes require six of eight signatures and a seven-day delay, while emergencies require seven signatures and can bypass the delay.

token_and_value_capture.body: The chain has no documented native token. Users pay gas in ETH, so early chain growth does not automatically create a new publicly traded asset. Robinhood may benefit through sequencer economics, brokerage activity, custody, trading and asset distribution, but the public data does not isolate those chain-level revenues. Stock tokens represent underlying products and should not be treated as network equity.

counterfactual.body: Robinhood could have used a public L2 without a dedicated chain, reducing fragmentation but giving up control over ordering and product rules. It could also open validation and sequencer participation earlier, improving neutrality while complicating launch operations. A native token could fund security or growth, but it would add regulation, dilution and speculation that the ETH-gas design currently avoids.

risks_and_unknowns.body: The chain is exposed to sequencer censorship, rapid upgrades, Security Council actions, permissioned validation, smart-contract failures and tokenized-asset legal restrictions. L2BEAT also identifies transaction-filtering controls. We do not know how many users return after launch promotions, what share of volume is economically independent or whether users can exit promptly during an operator or bridge failure.

lifecycle.body: Robinhood Chain is mixed because the evidence is strong but immature. More than $400 million of TVL and $14.72 billion of thirty-day DEX volume show a real launch, not an empty network. One month cannot establish retained demand, resilient exits or sustainable revenue, and key controls remain permissioned. The right label is early operating traction, not proven long-term success.

outlook_and_watch.body: The outlook improves if Robinhood converts brokerage distribution into repeat on-chain users, deeper stablecoins, diverse applications and orderly exits while opening validation. It weakens if volume falls after launch, tokenized assets face access limits or control remains concentrated. Watch weekly cohorts, non-Robinhood application share, stablecoin flows, fees, sequencer uptime, force-inclusion use, validator count and Security Council changes.

what_it_is.body: Arbitrum One is an Ethereum optimistic rollup running the Nitro stack. A centralized sequencer provides fast ordering, transaction data is posted to Ethereum and fraud proofs let validators challenge bad state claims. ETH pays gas. ARB governs the DAO but does not secure the rollup or pay transaction fees. Orbit chains such as Robinhood are separate networks and are not counted as Arbitrum One activity.

what_happened.body: Arbitrum became a major Ethereum DeFi venue, but capital and ARB price declined sharply from their peaks. TVL was $1.19 billion, down 71.72% from the October 2025 series peak. Dollar stablecoins were $3.59 billion and thirty-day DEX volume was $4.46 billion. ARB traded at $0.083, about 96.54% below its January 2024 recorded high.

why_this_outcome.body: EVM compatibility, Ethereum settlement, early DeFi liquidity and Nitro performance made Arbitrum an easy expansion path for applications and traders. BoLD and Stage 1 controls improved the exit and proof story. The weak part is value capture: users pay ETH, ARB mainly governs, and liquidity competes with Base, Optimism, Solana and app-specific chains. Strong usage therefore did not automatically support ARB valuation.

strategic_choices.body: Arbitrum chose a general-purpose rollup, Ethereum data availability, a centralized sequencer and DAO governance through ARB. It later shipped permissionless BoLD validation, Stylus and Timeboost ordering. A 2026 forum proposal would replace Timeboost with priority gas auctions, but it was still a proposal at review and must not be described as live policy. The system favors composability and staged decentralization over immediate full neutrality.

operating_model.body: The sequencer accepts and orders transactions for fast confirmation. Users can send through Ethereum if the sequencer censors them, subject to delays. Validators recompute state and BoLD disputes can challenge invalid assertions. Ethereum ultimately settles the rollup data and proof result. DAO governance and the Security Council can upgrade contracts, so technical exits coexist with governance trust.

token_and_value_capture.body: ARB gives holders governance power over DAO proposals, treasury and elected structures. It is not the gas token and is not staked to secure Arbitrum One, so chain use does not create mandatory ARB demand. CoinGecko observed a $546.71 million market capitalization and $826.59 million fully diluted value. That FDV gap and future unlocks matter, but public data does not prove how governance control should be valued.

counterfactual.body: Arbitrum could make ARB the gas or security asset, improving direct token demand while adding fee and regulatory complexity. It could decentralize sequencing faster, reducing censorship risk while weakening ordered-execution products and operational coordination. It could also retain more chain revenue for token holders, but governance rights and legal treatment would change. None of these alternatives guarantees more users.

risks_and_unknowns.body: Arbitrum still depends on a centralized sequencer, upgrade actors, the Security Council, Ethereum data availability and bridge contracts. ARB has weak direct value capture and continuing supply overhang. Aggregate volume does not show retained traders, organic fees or Orbit activity boundaries. We do not know how quickly sequencing will decentralize or whether DAO governance can resist voter apathy and delegate concentration.

lifecycle.body: Arbitrum is mixed. It remains a major rollup with $3.59 billion of stablecoins, $4.46 billion of thirty-day DEX volume and functioning Stage 1 exits. The 71.72% TVL drawdown and 96.54% ARB drawdown show that network relevance and token performance diverged. The chain is neither dead nor an unqualified success: product demand survived, while capital and value capture weakened.

outlook_and_watch.body: The call improves if Arbitrum retains developers and traders, grows stablecoins and fees, broadens sequencing and clarifies how DAO-controlled revenue benefits the ecosystem. It weakens if Base or app chains take distribution, governance concentrates or ARB unlocks outrun demand. Watch user cohorts, stablecoin net flows, DEX share, fees, sequencer uptime, forced-inclusion events, upgrade notices, delegates and ARB supply.

what_it_is.body: TRON is a delegated-proof-of-stake Layer 1 optimized for low-cost transfers and smart contracts. TRX holders stake and vote for Super Representatives; the top 27 produce blocks. Users consume bandwidth and energy obtained through staking or delegation, and burn TRX when resources are insufficient. TRON is best understood as a stablecoin payment rail with DeFi attached, not only as a DEX chain.

what_happened.body: TRON built the largest dollar-stablecoin balance in this cohort: $91.13 billion at review. TVL was $4.89 billion, down 66.80% from its December 2024 series peak, while thirty-day DEX volume was $1.12 billion. TRX traded at $0.329, 23.81% below its recorded high, far less impaired than many peer tokens. Stablecoin transfer use, not DEX volume, is the central demand story.

why_this_outcome.body: TRON won by making stablecoin transfers cheap, predictable and widely supported by exchanges and wallets. The stake-and-delegate resource model lets large senders prepay capacity instead of paying a volatile fee for every transfer. That distribution loop is difficult to dislodge. The tradeoff is concentrated governance and dependence on stablecoin issuers, exchanges and a narrow payments use case.

strategic_choices.body: TRON chose 27 elected block producers, a six-hour voting cycle and a two-resource fee model. It made TRX useful for staking, governance and buying capacity while burning TRX when users exceed allocated resources. This favors throughput and predictable transfer economics over a large rotating validator set. The network also prioritized stablecoin and exchange distribution rather than differentiated application infrastructure.

operating_model.body: TRX holders stake to receive voting power and bandwidth or energy. Votes select 27 Super Representatives every six hours; they produce blocks and receive block and voting rewards. Users can stake their own TRX, rent or receive delegated resources, or burn TRX for missing capacity. Smart contracts consume energy while ordinary transactions consume bandwidth.

token_and_value_capture.body: TRX pays for scarce bandwidth and energy, is staked for resources and votes, and funds block and voting rewards. Resource shortfalls burn TRX while protocol rewards mint it, so net supply depends on real usage versus issuance. CoinGecko observed a $31.18 billion market capitalization and similar fully diluted value. Stablecoin balances support blockspace demand, but the stablecoins belong to their issuers and holders, not TRX holders.

counterfactual.body: TRON could expand the validator set or use more permissionless block production, reducing control concentration while potentially weakening speed and coordination. It could diversify beyond stablecoin transfers, reducing issuer dependence but diluting its best distribution advantage. It could also move more fees directly to validators instead of burning TRX, improving operator revenue while weakening token scarcity.

risks_and_unknowns.body: TRON depends heavily on stablecoin issuers and exchange distribution. Twenty-seven block producers create governance, censorship and correlated-operator risk, while entity overlap among producers is not established by the public rulebook. Legal and reputation risk persists; a 2026 SEC release concerned a proposed settlement of specific Rainberry allegations, not a finding that current TRON transactions are wash trading.

lifecycle.body: TRON is thriving within a narrow role. Its $91.13 billion stablecoin balance, $31.18 billion TRX market value and relatively modest 23.81% token drawdown show durable payment demand. TVL remains 66.80% below peak and DEX volume is not dominant, so the success is not broad DeFi leadership. The chain works because it became a distribution rail for stablecoins.

outlook_and_watch.body: The outlook improves if stablecoin transfers remain sticky, issuers diversify, resource demand keeps TRX net-deflationary and producer control broadens. It weakens if major issuers or exchanges migrate rails, regulation limits access or producer entities concentrate. Watch stablecoin balances and transfer volume separately, issuer share, resource burns, reward issuance, active senders, fees and entity-grouped Super Representative votes.

what_it_is.body: Avalanche is a proof-of-stake platform whose Primary Network contains the X-Chain, P-Chain and EVM-compatible C-Chain. It also supports sovereign Avalanche L1s with their own validator sets and rules. Those L1s are not rollups and their activity should not be silently counted as C-Chain activity. AVAX secures the Primary Network, pays its fees and is used for continuing L1 validator fees.

what_happened.body: Avalanche kept a live C-Chain and expanded its sovereign-L1 strategy, but its market footprint remains far below the 2021 peak. TVL was $435.81 million, down 96.21% from the December 2021 series maximum. Dollar stablecoins were $1.50 billion and thirty-day DEX volume was $1.30 billion. AVAX traded at $6.57, about 95.47% below its recorded high.

why_this_outcome.body: Fast finality, EVM compatibility and early incentive programs brought DeFi capital in 2021. Much of that capital left when incentives and the market cycle faded. Avalanche then emphasized custom institutional and application chains. Etna cut the cost of launching those L1s, but it also separated their validators and economics from C-Chain. The strategy created optionality without yet restoring broad capital or AVAX valuation.

strategic_choices.body: Avalanche chose three coordinated Primary Network chains, an EVM C-Chain and horizontally scaled sovereign L1s rather than one globally shared execution layer. Etna removed the requirement that each L1 validator also stake 2,000 AVAX on the Primary Network and replaced it with a continuous AVAX fee. The upgrade lowered launch costs and C-Chain fee floors, trading tighter shared security for application-specific control.

operating_model.body: Primary Network validators stake at least 2,000 AVAX for two weeks to one year and validate the X-, P- and C-Chains. Correct participation earns minted AVAX rewards; negligent validators lose potential rewards but are not slashed. The P-Chain manages validators and sovereign L1 registrations, the C-Chain runs EVM applications and each Avalanche L1 chooses its own validator and execution rules.

token_and_value_capture.body: AVAX pays Primary Network fees, secures validators, is burned when fees are paid and serves as the continuing fee asset for registered L1 validators. Supply is capped at 720 million, but validator rewards mint new AVAX, so the asset can remain inflationary while usage burns less than issuance. CoinGecko observed a $2.84 billion market capitalization and $3.04 billion fully diluted value.

counterfactual.body: Avalanche could require every application chain to share Primary Network validators, strengthening common security and AVAX staking demand while making chains more expensive to launch. It could focus only on C-Chain, concentrating liquidity but giving up custom-chain differentiation. It could slash validators for faults, increasing penalties while adding operational and governance risk around mistakes.

risks_and_unknowns.body: Avalanche faces thin C-Chain liquidity relative to peak, AVAX dilution, fragmented application-chain liquidity and different security for every sovereign L1. A chain labeled Avalanche may not be secured by the Primary Network validator set. We do not have a single reconciled view of C-Chain users, L1 users, validator ownership, cross-chain bridge exposure or how much L1 growth produces net AVAX demand.

lifecycle.body: Avalanche is mixed. It still supports $1.50 billion of stablecoins, $1.30 billion of thirty-day DEX volume and active sovereign-L1 development. The 96.21% TVL drawdown and 95.47% AVAX drawdown show that the 2021 valuation and liquidity thesis did not persist. The network has a differentiated architecture and live use, but current evidence does not support a return to broad DeFi leadership.

outlook_and_watch.body: The outlook improves if sovereign L1s attract recurring users and fees, C-Chain liquidity stabilizes and continuous L1 fees plus transaction burns offset AVAX issuance. It weakens if custom chains fragment liquidity without durable demand or avoid meaningful AVAX use. Watch L1 launches and retained users, C-Chain stablecoins and DEX share, AVAX burns versus rewards, validator ownership, interchain transfers and security incidents by chain.
